analysis.one_liner: Lets patients get the abortion pill mifepristone by telehealth visit and by mail.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Food and Drug Administration to change the special safety restrictions (called a REMS) that apply to mifepristone, the drug approved for medication abortion. It would have removed the requirement that patients pick up the drug in person, allowed prescriptions through telehealth appointments, and let any certified pharmacy mail the drug to patients. At the time, the FDA had already said its own data supported dropping the in-person requirement, and had suspended enforcing it during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients seeking medication abortion, especially those in states that have restricted abortion and those far from a certified provider. Under the bill, they could consult a doctor by video and receive the drug by mail instead of traveling to a certified clinic or provider in person. Certified pharmacies that dispense mifepristone would gain a new mail-order role, and telehealth providers could serve patients they currently cannot reach.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone from the drug's safety strategy, so patients no longer have to travel to a certified provider to pick it up.
Allows patients to access prescriptions for mifepristone via telehealth appointments.
Permits any pharmacy certified to dispense mifepristone to dispense and mail it to patients.
The bill preserves the FDA's authority to later eliminate the REMS entirely if sound scientific evidence supports it.

analysis.who_pays: The bill has no direct taxpayer cost. The burden would fall on the mifepristone application holder, which must submit the modified safety plan, and on the safety-oversight system: opponents argue that removing in-person screening eliminates a chance to catch complications, confirm gestational age, or identify coercion before the drug is dispensed.
analysis.who_pays_short: The drug's manufacturer and safety-oversight protocols

drawbacks.text: Removing the in-person dispensing requirement eliminates an in-person medical checkpoint before the drug is taken; critics of loosened mifepristone rules argue this screening catches risks and coercion that a telehealth visit cannot.

The bill is written as a mandate on the FDA and the drug's sponsor rather than a neutral review: it requires a specific outcome (telehealth access and mail dispensing) rather than leaving the safety decision entirely to the agency, though it preserves the agency's authority to scrap the REMS altogether on scientific grounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients — particularly in states where abortion is now restricted or where the nearest certified provider is hours away — the benefit of telehealth and mail access is substantial and concrete. The cost is the loss of an in-person checkpoint that some clinicians consider a safety safeguard, though the FDA itself had stated that its data supported removing the in-person requirement and had stopped enforcing it during the COVID-19 emergency. The mandate structure, dictating the REMS outcome by statute, is a legitimate design criticism even for supporters.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Cori Bush introduced the bill on July 18, 2022, with five Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action — no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote — was ever taken on the bill.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No concentrated interest gained directly. The practical result was that the more restrictive status quo stayed in place: mifepristone remained subject to the in-person dispensing requirement in federal rule, and patients in restricted states were left without a federal guarantee of telehealth or mail access.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo and its restrictions

for.name: Rep. Cori Bush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to remove the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone and allow telehealth and mail access.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or hearing, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat, no Republican sponsored or supported the bill, and there were no votes at which a party split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would allow any certified pharmacy to dispense and mail mifepristone, opening a new dispensing role and revenue stream. That expansion is also what delivers mail access to patients, so the industry's gain here runs alongside patients' access.
Telehealth visits would become a lawful channel for prescribing mifepristone, expanding the telehealth abortion market. The same change is what lets patients avoid traveling to a certified provider.

The application holder must bear the cost of drafting the modified safety plan, but a loosened REMS enlarges the pool of patients who can obtain the drug. The bill preserves the FDA's power to eliminate the REMS entirely if the science supports it.
